                    ### Question
                    A 55-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and worsening abdominal pain for 4 weeks. He also reports excessive night sweats and a 5.4-kg (12-lb) weight loss during this time. He has a neck swelling for 4 days. Physical examination shows a nontender, enlarged, and fixed supraclavicular lymph node. There is splenomegaly. A CT scan of the thorax and abdomen shows massively enlarged axillary, mediastinal, and cervical lymph nodes. Analysis of an excised cervical lymph node shows lymphocytes with a high proliferative index that stain positive for CD20. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Adult T-cell lymphoma
opb. Burkitt lymphoma
opc. Follicular lymphoma
opd. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
ope. Hodgkin lymphoma

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with systemic symptoms including fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, and an enlarged, fixed supraclavicular lymph node, along with splenomegaly. A CT scan reveals extensive lymphadenopathy, and the lymph node biopsy shows lymphocytes with a high proliferative index that are CD20 positive, indicating a B-cell origin. These findings are most consistent with Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), which is the most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults and typically presents with aggressive symptoms and significant lymphadenopathy. Other options such as Hodgkin lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma are less likely given the age, presentation, and biopsy results. The evidence paths related to CD20 positivity and lymphocyte proliferation support the diagnosis of DLBCL.
